There are approximately 5,000 speakers. p, t, k, b, d, g, q (glottal), m, n, ng, s, w, y are the consonant phonemes. i, a, o, e (mid-back unround) are the vowel phonemes. There are two syllable patterns CV, and CVC. There is also a phoneme of stress symbolized by '. [Reid ed. 1971:18] 18. Itneg, Binongan (ItgB.) List supplied by Charles Walton (SIL). Unpublished paper in SIL Philippines files (1965). Consonants: p t k q / b d g / m n ng / s / l / w y Vowels: i ë (ɨ) o / a Stress ... Pronouns ... diya'kɨn dika'mi / di'ka dika'yo / di'ta dita'yo / kan si'ya kaday'da ... Demonstratives I. a. kanto'wɨ II. a. sito'wɨ / b. kan'ta b. si'ta / c. kandi'yɨ c. sidi'yɨ [Reid ed. 1971, introduction p. x] q represents glottal stop. new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is treated as a phoneme, i.e. contrastive and lexically specified (marked with an acute/apostrophe-like accent in the phonemic transcription); the source gives no default position, no distributional restriction (e.g. penult vs. final), and no rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the note is a one-sentence inventory statement. The published interlinear texts in the same paper (and J. Walton 1975) are in a practical orthography that does not mark stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level phonemic inventory statement in a footnote to a discourse (paragraph-structure) description; no discussion of phrase-level prominence or citation forms. A fuller phoneme chart for Binongan Itneg by the same author is in Reid (ed.) 1971, not accessible here.
new_statements.identity_note: C. Walton 1971 describes 'the Binongan Itneg dialect.. spoken in the Municipality of Licuan-Baay, in Abra Province' (data from barrio Nalbuan, Baay, 1963-68) = bino1237 exactly. Reid 1974/1973 'Itneg' data are also Walton's Binongan material, but Reid 1974 additionally discusses Inlaod and Masadiit Itneg (other Itneg varieties: inla1263? / masa1300), and Reid 2006 cites 'Lacub Itneg' from Yamada & Tsuchida 1975 (Lacub municipality is within the Binongan Itneg area per Ethnologue, but that identification is not stated in the source).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is listed as a phoneme of Binongan Itneg (no placement rule is given). In the word list, which marks stress with an apostrophe before the stressed syllable, Binongan Itneg forms carry stress on either the penult ('qobit 'anus', 'balat, 'qokis, 'libo, 'qiplog) or the final syllable (bo'wa 'areca nut', naba'qin 'ashamed', ma'digos, ta'big, bi'kin, qa'nak, ta'lo), so placement is contrastive/lexical, the usual Philippine penult-vs-final pattern, with no rule stated in the source.
new_statements.exceptions: none stated; the source gives no rule, only a phoneme 'Stress' and marked word-list forms
new_statements.identity_note: Reid 1971 p. 18 states that the Binongan Itneg list 'represents the dialect spoken in the Ba-ay Valley' (Licuan-Baay, Abra), also called Tinguian; this is the same variety as Walton 1971 (Municipality of Licuan-Baay). The listed open_url (rosettaproject_ilk_phon-1) describes Ilongot (Kakiduge:n Bugkalut), a different language.
